According to Buddhism, hell does exist as a realm within the cycle of rebirth. [d2] identifies Naraka (hellish) as one of the realms of rebirth, stating that "bad karma is believed to produce rebirth which is more unhappy and evil." [d8] further specifies that niraya (hell) is one of four planes below the human plane in a cosmology of thirty-one planes of existence, and that "beings are born into these states as a result of their unwholesome kamma." [d3] describes the World of Hell (jigoku, Sanskrit naraka) as "the lowest state of life, a state in which one is imprisoned by suffering and completely lacking in freedom," with Buddhist scriptures describing many hells, including eight hot hells and eight cold hells. [d7] adds that for Buddhists, rebirth in the hell-realm is "a consequence of how we use our minds," not a divine judgment. [d4] notes that unlike monotheistic versions, Buddhist hell is not permanent — "there is a way to leave the Buddhist ones, but it takes a long time and extraordinary effort." Some schools, such as the Yogācāra (Mind-Only) school [d4] and Nichiren Buddhism [d3], also interpret hell as an inner state of mind rather than solely a physical location.
